title: ExeGPT: Constraint-Aware Resource Scheduling for LLM Inference
technique: Offline branch-and-bound search (monotonic optimization over XSimulator estimates) for batch sizes, decoder micro-batches, partial tensor parallelism and encoding frequency under two policies (RRA, WAA) that maximize throughput subject to a latency bound; reschedules when sequence-length distribution drifts

optimized_metrics.evidence: Our optimization problem is to maximize the inference throughput under a given latency constraint by finding the optimal values of the control variables for the given scheduling policy.
LBound is the latency bound for the given sequence length.
optimized_metrics.locator: §5 problem formulation; §7.1: 'we used the sequence length at the 99th percentile (pctl in short) in the distribution'
optimized_metrics.stat_quote: we applied the same latency bound to generating ... the 99th pctl in the distribution.

headline_claim.text: Compared to FasterTransformer, ExeGPT achieves up to 15.2× improvements in throughput and 6× improvements in latency. Overall, ExeGPT achieves an average throughput gain of 2.9× across twenty evaluation scenarios.

reported_metrics.where: Figs 11-12 (99th percentile latency of all queries under distribution shift)

metric_definitions.definition_quote: LB is for generating 99th pctl-length sequence.
metric_definitions.notes: Latency = time to run encode+decode for one sequence of the 99th-percentile output length (worst-case execution), i.e. a bound on per-sequence generation time, set per model/task.

metric_definitions.definition_quote: We assumed two specific SLAs for the latency constraint: (a) ensuring that 99% of all queries are completed within a given timeframe and (b) ensuring that a sequence of a prespecified length (e.g. 99th pctl-length) is completed within a given time constraint.
metric_definitions.notes: Paper notes no LLM provider defines explicit latency constraints in SLAs; these are introduced for evaluation.
Sequences per second (output sequences, not tokens); not formally defined otherwise. Synthetic sequences are forced to fixed generated lengths (no EOS).

slo_spec: Four latency bounds per task from FasterTransformer runs: bottom 10%, 30%, 70% of FT latencies across batch sizes, and infinity; bound applied to generating the 99th-percentile-length sequence (worst-case).
load_regime: synthetic input/output length distributions (truncated normal) with decoding forced to given length; throughput at a latency bound; no arrival process
tradeoff_acknowledged: Larger batch / fewer micro-batches raises throughput at the cost of latency; under distribution shift a non-adjusted schedule can violate the latency constraint.
hardware: A40 cluster (48 GPUs, PCIe) and A100 cluster (16 GPUs, NVLink)
models: T5, OPT, GPT-3 (six configs, up to 175B)
workloads: summarization, translation, code generation, two conversational QA tasks; synthetic length distributions based on datasets; a subset on WMT, Alpaca, CNN
extractor_notes: TAIL IN CONSTRAINT: the latency bound is a worst-case / 99th-percentile-LENGTH sequence latency (not a percentile of measured request latencies), except SLA (a) in the shift experiment (99% of queries within a timeframe). Objective is throughput, so the paper is not a tail-latency optimizer. No online arrivals or queueing: scheduler assumes a saturated stream, hence load_class offline-batch (steady-state throughput, no queueing delay in latency). 'latency 6x improvement' is at equal throughput vs FasterTransformer.
load_class_quote: we generated input/output sequences with truncated normal distribution using average and variance parameters that reflect those of the datasets corresponding to the tasks.
